commands.control: Falco is watching; plain recon matches no rule
commands.explain: You are an unprivileged user (uid 10001) in a hardened pod. Falco sees this and lets it pass - looking around is not, by itself, an attack.

commands.control: Falco is watching; plain recon matches no rule
commands.explain: The pod name, nothing more. No node name, no cluster detail - the pod was built without that information to leak.

commands.control: Falco is watching; plain recon matches no rule
commands.explain: Only the shop server and your own command run here: one container, one job, nothing else to pivot to.

commands.control: Falco is watching; plain recon matches no rule
commands.explain: The shop's files, writable by you because this directory is the one writable spot in the pod. Note the .flag - that is a goal.

commands.control: Pod Security: runs non-root, holds no Linux capabilities
commands.explain: CapEff is all zeros: the pod runs as a non-root user and holds no Linux capabilities at all. That is why the next few tricks will not work.

commands.control: Falco is watching; an app rewriting its own files is not drift
commands.explain: The shop window next to you just changed - you rewrote its page and its status. Nothing stopped you: writing to your own working directory is normal for an app, so no rule here watches for it.

commands.control: Falco is watching; reading a file you can already open is not flagged
commands.explain: You found this run's flag. Reading it was allowed - but detection is not prevention, and reading a secret inside the pod is not the same as getting it out past a default-deny network.

commands.control: Falco rule Read sensitive file untrusted -> terminate
commands.explain: Falco caught an untrusted program opening the password database and Talon deleted the pod. What you got was worthless anyway: every account in the image is locked, there is no hash in the file.

commands.control: Read-only root filesystem (pod hardening, not required by PSS)
commands.explain: "Read-only file system." The container's root filesystem is mounted read-only, so you cannot plant a backdoor in /bin. Nothing had to kill you - the write simply never happened.

commands.control: Pod Security: no ServiceAccount token mounted
commands.explain: "No such file or directory." There is no token to steal: the pod was created with none, so it cannot talk to the Kubernetes API no matter what you run.

commands.control: Pod Security: non-root user, no CAP_CHOWN
commands.explain: "Operation not permitted." Changing a file's owner needs CAP_CHOWN, which only root holds; the pod runs as a non-root user with no capabilities, so a whole class of tricks is off the table before any rule has to fire.

commands.control: Falco rule SDP network tool in sandbox -> quarantine
commands.explain: A network tool started: Falco flagged it and Talon quarantined the pod. The run goes on - you still have a shell - but Cilium has cut every connection, both ways, so the shop next to you just went unreachable. You are trapped with nothing to call out to.

commands.control: Falco rule Terminal shell in container -> terminate
commands.explain: A second interactive shell with a terminal attached is exactly the signature Falco watches for; Talon deleted the pod within a second or two. This ends your run.

commands.control: Falco rule SDP execution from shop volume -> terminate
commands.explain: You copied a binary into the writable shop volume and ran it. The stock drift rule misses this - that volume is not the container's overlay layer - so a custom rule watches for execution from it. Falco caught it and Talon deleted the pod.
